what.text: Sermorelin is a 29-amino-acid version of human growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH). It is the shortest synthetic peptide with the full activity of GHRH. It acts on the pituitary gland to release growth hormone.

As Geref (EMD Serono), it was FDA approved as an injection in 1990 to test whether the pituitary can release growth hormone, and in 1997 to treat idiopathic growth hormone deficiency in children with growth failure. The maker discontinued both products in 2008 and asked FDA to withdraw the approvals.

src.label: FDA, Determination that GEREF (sermorelin acetate) was not withdrawn for safety or effectiveness, 78 FR 14095

what.text: What Adonis carries through Beluga, all compounded: a sermorelin troche dissolved in the mouth; sermorelin with glycine as a tablet taken by mouth; sermorelin oral strips dissolved on the tongue; and sermorelin given by injection.
Sermorelin for sleep or longevity is off-label. It was never approved for either, and those uses have barely been studied.

research.text: We found no trial of sermorelin with sleep or longevity as its result, and no published human study of sermorelin by mouth, troche or strip. What exists are small 1990s studies in older adults that measured growth hormone and IGF-1, and a few studies of natural GHRH and sleep.
Each is listed below as it was run.

research.title: GH and IGF-1 in older men, 1992 (USA, NIA)

facts.v: older men took a low and a high dose of GHRH-(1-29) under the skin twice daily, in random order, 14 days each, with a 14-day break. Young men were measured once for comparison. No placebo.
10 healthy older men (mean age 68) and 9 young men (mean age 26)
24-hour growth hormone release, IGF-1, glucose, blood pressure, blood tests

research.found: At the high dose only, growth hormone and IGF-1 rose to levels not different from the young men. Glucose, blood pressure and blood tests did not change. Body composition, sleep and lifespan were not measured.

src.label: Corpas et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab, 1992

research.meta: USA · 1997 · Open study, no control group
research.title: Nightly injections in older men, 1997 (USA)

facts.v: before-and-after study, no placebo. Nightly self-injections of GHRH (1-29) under the skin.
11 healthy men aged 64 to 76 with low IGF-1
night-time growth hormone, IGF-1, muscle strength and energy use, body composition, glucose, lipids

research.found: Night-time growth hormone rose, but IGF-1 did not change. Two of six strength measures and one endurance test improved. Weight, muscle, fat, glucose and lipids did not change. No significant adverse effects were seen.

research.title: A related analogue in older adults, 1997 (USA)

facts.v: single-blind. Nightly saline injections for 4 weeks, then 16 weeks of [Nle27]GHRH-(1-29)-NH2, a modified analogue, not sermorelin itself.
growth hormone, IGF-1, body composition, skin thickness, insulin sensitivity, quality of life including sleep

research.found: IGF-1 rose within 2 weeks and drifted back toward baseline by 16 weeks. Skin thickness rose in both sexes; lean mass rose in men only. Sleep quality was unaffected in both sexes. The only side effect was a transient rise in blood lipids.

src.label: Khorram et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab, 1997

research.title: Combined peptides in men on testosterone, 2017 (USA)

facts.v: retrospective review of records. Men took sermorelin together with GHRP-2 and GHRP-6, so sermorelin’s own effect cannot be separated.
105 men reviewed; 14 met strict inclusion criteria (mean age 33)

research.found: Mean IGF-1 rose from 159.5 to 239.0 ng/mL. Sleep and longevity were not measured.

src.label: Sigalos et al., Am J Mens Health, 2017

research.text: GHRH and sleep (form not named as sermorelin)

items.text: double-blind crossover, one night each. 12 young and 11 older healthy men got GHRH or placebo by nasal spray before bed, with sleep recorded. GHRH increased REM sleep and slow-wave sleep in the second half of the night, at both ages. The abstract does not say whether the GHRH was sermorelin.

13 healthy older adults (mean age 69) got GHRH or placebo by vein during the night. GHRH reduced night-time awakenings, but the authors said it promoted sleep much less than in young people. The abstract does not say which form of GHRH was used.
a University of Washington trial of GHRH for age-related sleep problems in older men and women started in 1996 and was completed in 2007. No results are posted on the registry.

research.text: Children with growth hormone deficiency (the approved use)
A 1999 review says limited data showed nightly sermorelin injections raised growth speed in some children with idiopathic growth hormone deficiency, by less than growth hormone itself.

us.text: Sermorelin was once FDA approved, as Geref. Both approvals were withdrawn in 2009 at the maker’s request, and FDA later found they were not withdrawn for safety or effectiveness reasons. No sermorelin product is FDA approved today. As of October 31, 2026.

us.text: The sermorelin troche, tablet with glycine, oral strips and injection that Adonis carries through Beluga are compounded. They are not FDA approved. Using sermorelin for sleep or longevity is off-label.
Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved. FDA does not review their safety, effectiveness or quality before they are sold.

after.title: Sport
after.text: Sermorelin is prohibited at all times (in and out of competition) under WADA class S2.2.4, growth hormone releasing factors, which names “growth hormone-releasing hormone (GHRH) and its analogues (e.g. CJC-1293, CJC-1295, sermorelin and tesamorelin).” Substances in S2 are non-Specified. It is still named on the 2027 list, in force January 1, 2027.

side.text: Geref’s label is not available on Drugs@FDA, so the points below come from the studies and records we could open. They are small and short.

items.text: a 1999 review reports that transient facial flushing and pain at the injection site were the most common adverse events.

one 6-week study saw no significant adverse effects. A 14-day study saw no change in glucose, blood pressure or blood tests. A 5-month study of a related analogue saw a transient rise in blood lipids.

src.label: Corpas et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab, 1992
Khorram et al., J Clin Endocrinol Metab, 1997

items.text: compounded sermorelin vials have been recalled for being out of specification. FDA’s recall notice says products with more or less drug than labeled may cause lower effect or unintended side effects.
we found no safety data for sermorelin taken by mouth, as a troche or as a strip, or for long-term use for sleep or aging.

unconfirmed: Geref's FDA label (warnings and side effects) is not available on Drugs@FDA and could not be opened.
We could not find an FDA statement on whether 503A pharmacies may compound sermorelin as a component of an approved drug now that Geref's approvals are withdrawn.
The 1997 and 1999 GHRH sleep studies and the registered University of Washington sleep trial do not name the GHRH form used, so they may not have used sermorelin.
We found no published human study of sermorelin given by mouth, as a troche or as a strip.
Status in the UK, EU and Australia was not checked against a regulator record.
surprises: Sermorelin is often described as FDA approved; FDA withdrew both Geref approvals effective June 18, 2009 at the maker's request (not for safety), and every sermorelin product sold today is compounded and unapproved.
The one GHRH-analogue trial in older adults that asked about sleep (Khorram 1997) found sleep quality unaffected.
Compounded sermorelin is prescribed for “age management” (per an FDA-posted recall notice), yet WADA bans it at all times as a non-Specified S2 substance.
